title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: Float is only free if your combined ratio stays below 100; otherwise, you are paying to borrow.
epigraph.author: Insurance Economics Axiom

web_blocks.html: An insurer's 'supply chain' is a capital and risk-transfer pipeline: distribution (acquiring risk), underwriting & pricing (selecting and structuring risk), reinsurance cession (hedging tail risk), claims & reserving (settling losses), and float management (investing policyholder funds until claims are paid). Chubb distributes commercial and HNW personal lines primarily through independent retail brokers (Marsh, Aon, Gallagher, regional agencies) and wholesale E&S brokers via Westchester. Overseas General and Chubb Life utilize tied agents, direct-to-consumer digital/telemarketing, and bancassurance partnerships across Asia and Latin America [1, 4, 14]. Because Chubb's brand and claims service carry high retention among middle-market and affluent clients, broker relationships function as a sticky, mutually profitable distribution moat.

To protect its $73.76 billion shareholders' equity from extreme tail events, Chubb cedes roughly 16.9% of its gross premiums written ($65.95B GPW vs. $54.84B NPW in FY2025) to third-party reinsurers [2]. When a major catastrophe exhausts a reinsurance layer—as occurred during the Q1 2025 Southern California wildfires—Chubb pays reinstatement premiums ($50 million ceded in 2025) to restore catastrophe protection for the remainder of the treaty year [12]. On the asset side, Chubb held $168.7 billion in total invested assets at year-end 2025 against $88.02 billion in gross unpaid losses ($69.67B net of $18.35B reinsurance recoverables) [1, 14]. Its fixed-income portfolio (ex-Huatai) carried a 5.1% book yield, a 5.5% market yield, and a conservative 4.7–4.8 year duration, generating $6,465 million in pre-tax net investment income ($6,950 million adjusted) in FY2025 [1, 2, 14].

web_blocks.caption: Chubb Limited FY2025 Consolidated Unit Economics Waterfall ($ Millions; Audited 10-K Basis)
web_blocks.takeaway: On $59,402M of consolidated revenue ($53,014M net premiums earned + $6,465M net investment income - $77M net realized/other), Chubb retained $10,622M in consolidated net income ($10,310M attributable to Chubb) and converted it into $12,820M of operating cash flow (120.7% cash conversion) [1, 14].

web_blocks.html: The unit economics of Chubb's P&C business are governed by the combined ratio: in FY2025, every $100 of net premiums earned absorbed roughly $58.20 in losses and loss-adjustment expenses (including $5.50 of catastrophe losses and -$2.10 of favorable prior-year reserve releases) and $27.50 in policy acquisition and administrative expenses, leaving $14.30 in pure underwriting profit (85.7% combined ratio) [1, 2, 4]. Because Chubb earns an underwriting profit before investment income, its $69.67 billion of net loss reserves—plus unearned premiums and life reserves—effectively function as negative-cost float, compounding investment income on top of underwriting gains. In turn, Chubb's expense ratio benefits from scale: administrative expenses of $4,504 million represent just 8.5% of net premiums earned ($53,014M). This gives chubb a structural cost advantage over smaller regional carriers [1].

Chubb's distribution architecture is deliberately multi-channel so the company is never captive to a single intermediary [1, 14]. Large corporate and multinational accounts flow through global wholesale and retail brokers (Marsh, Aon, Gallagher, WTW). There, chubb's $168.7B balance sheet and AA / A++ ratings make it a mandatory lead-line market [6, 7]. Middle-market commercial and affluent personal lines flow through thousands of independent regional agents who rely on Chubb's proprietary underwriting portals, local branch underwriters, and high-touch claims service.

Internationally, Chubb pairs independent brokers with direct-to-consumer digital partnerships and bank-assurance alliances across Asia and Latin America. This allows low-acquisition-cost A&H and life distribution [1, 14]. On the claims side, Chubb's in-house claims organization handles the vast majority of complex losses directly rather than outsourcing to third-party administrators, preserving loss-adjustment expense (LAE) discipline and preventing claims leakage.

Reinsurance cession and catastrophe aggregate management represent the invisible half of Chubb's unit economics [1, 14]. Rather than retaining unlimited tail risk on coastal windstorm or California wildfire exposures, Chubb purchases structured catastrophe reinsurance treaties and utilizes per-occurrence and aggregate retentions calibrated to protect its statutory surplus and A++ rating [7, 14]. During the January 2025 Southern California wildfires—which caused $1.47B in pre-tax catastrophe losses for Chubb—the company's diversified earnings base and reinsurance structure absorbed the shock while still delivering a record-low 85.7% full-year P&C combined ratio [2, 12].

Equally important is Chubb's investment-portfolio duration and asset-liability matching (ALM). By keeping fixed-income duration at 4.7–4.8 years (ex-Huatai) and holding overwhelmingly investment-grade corporate, municipal, and government bonds, Chubb avoids reaching for illiquid private-credit or equity-heavy beta that could force capital dilution during a market downturn [2, 3, 14].

On the expense-ratio front, Chubb's scale allows continuous investment in commercial underwriting workbenches, automated small-commercial policy issuance, and AI-assisted claims triage without inflating its ~25%–26% P&C expense ratio [1, 14]. Smaller regional competitors lack the premium volume to amortize modern policy-administration and catastrophe-modeling platforms. This gives chubb a durable 200–400 basis point structural cost advantage in middle-market commercial lines.
Good float is free or negative-cost funding. Chubb earns an underwriting profit before investing a dime. Its bond book then earns 5.1% to 5.5% on top. That dual engine drives cash flow.
Brokers, agents, and bank partners all sell Chubb policies. No single channel controls the price. In-house claims teams keep loss costs tight and clients loyal.
Clean cost control ties the model together. Low losses and steady bond income work side by side. Shareholders keep more cash as a result.

book_paragraphs: When you and I examine an insurer's unit economics, we shouldn't look for factories or warehouses—we should trace the pipeline of risk and cash. At Chubb, that pipeline has five stages: distribution, underwriting, reinsurance, claims reserving, and float investing.

On distribution, Chubb meets corporate and affluent clients primarily through major global brokers like Marsh and Aon, regional independent agencies, and wholesale excess-and-surplus brokers—while overseas and in Asia Life, it layers in bancassurance partnerships and tied agents. In 2025, that network brought in $65.95 billion of gross premiums. Chubb didn't keep all of it: it ceded roughly 17% to reinsurers, leaving $54.84 billion in net premiums written. That cession is the company's shock absorber—and when a giant event like the January 2025 California wildfires hits, Chubb pays a $50 million reinstatement premium to reload its catastrophe cover for the rest of the year.

Claims management is the next critical link. When a loss occurs, Chubb's in-house claims adjusters and legal teams determine whether to settle or litigate, while actuaries book unpaid loss reserves—which stood at $88.02 billion gross ($69.67 billion net of $18.35 billion in reinsurance recoverables) at year-end 2025. Because long-tail casualty claims can take five to ten years to settle, Chubb holds those reserves in its investment portfolio during the interim.

Now look at the FY2025 income-to-cash waterfall. Chubb generated $59,402 million in total revenue—$53,014 million in net premiums earned plus $6,465 million in net investment income, less $77 million in minor realized/other items. Out of that, $31,243 million went to P&C losses, loss-adjustment expenses, and life policy benefits; $9,847 million went to broker commissions and policy acquisition costs; $4,504 million covered administrative and underwriting staff expenses; and $764 million paid debt interest. After $2,422 million in income taxes, Chubb banked $10,622 million in consolidated net income ($10,310 million attributable to Chubb shareholders)—and converted that into $12,820 million in operating cash flow.

Here is why that math is so powerful: because Chubb's P&C combined ratio was 85.7%, it collected $14.30 of underwriting profit on every $100 of earned premium before earning a single dime on its investments. That means Chubb's $168.7 billion investment portfolio—yielding 5.1% on book and 5.5% at market with a conservative 4.7-to-4.8 year duration—is funded by negative-cost float. And notice the operating leverage: administrative expenses were just $4.50 billion against $53.01 billion in earned premiums, an 8.5% administrative ratio that smaller rivals simply cannot match.

Let us trace how a dollar of premium actually travels through Chubb's distribution and balance sheet plumbing, because that $100 waterfall in Chapter 3 reveals the entire secret of insurance compounding. When a broker places a $100 commercial policy with Chubb, roughly $60 to $62 goes toward expected loss and loss-adjustment expenses, and another $24 to $26 covers broker commissions, underwriting salaries, and technology overhead. That leaves $12 to $15 of pure underwriting profit before Chubb earns a single dime on its investments.

Think about how rare that is. Most average insurers run a 97% to 101% combined ratio, meaning they barely break even—or actually lose money—on underwriting just to get their hands on policyholder float. Chubb gets paid $12 to $15 per $100 of premium just to hold the float! Then it invests that $168.7 billion float into high-grade corporate, municipal, and sovereign bonds yielding over 5.1%, compounding operating cash flow at more than 120% of net income.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Most investors focus on combined ratio alone, or investment income alone. Chubb's edge is the flywheel between them: $12.82 billion in annual operating cash flow pouring into a 5.5% market-yield bond portfolio while underwriting stays 14 points below breakeven.

book_subsections.title: Float Mechanics, Asset-Liability Matching & Claims Discipline
paragraphs: You hear investors talk casually about insurance float, as if all float were created equal. It is not. Float generated at a 103% combined ratio is expensive debt—you are paying 3% a year just to borrow policyholders' money, which forces your investment team to stretch for risky yields in junk bonds, private equity, or commercial real estate to break even. Float generated at an 85.7% combined ratio is negative-cost capital: policyholders are effectively paying Chubb 14.3 cents on the dollar to hold their reserves until claims come due.

Because Chubb earns such a wide underwriting margin, its chief investment officer does not have to be a hero. Chubb holds roughly $168.7 billion in invested assets, overwhelmingly concentrated in investment-grade fixed-income securities with an average credit rating of A/AA and a duration of 4.7 to 4.8 years. As older 3% and 4% bonds mature each quarter, Chubb reinvests the proceeds at 5.5% market yields, steadily lifting the portfolio's 5.1% book yield.

Meanwhile, on the distribution side, Chubb's multi-channel reach—spanning global brokers like Marsh and Aon for Fortune 500 accounts, thousands of independent regional agents for middle-market and Masterpiece policies, and Asian bancassurance and digital partnerships—ensures that no single distributor holds pricing leverage over Chubb.

book_subsections.title: Technology, Actuarial Scale & Expense-Ratio Leverage
paragraphs: In commercial insurance, scale is not just about writing bigger policies—it is about how cheaply you can process a million small and mid-sized ones. Every year, Chubb processes millions of quotes, endorsements, and claims across 54 countries. Because its $54.84 billion premium base spreads technology and actuarial data-science costs over an enormous denominator, Chubb can afford proprietary catastrophe models and automated small-commercial underwriting portals that a $2 billion regional carrier simply cannot fund.

The result shows up in a lean ~25% to 26% expense ratio alongside industry-leading loss selection. Even when pricing softens in large-account property, that structural expense advantage keeps Chubb solidly profitable while higher-cost rivals dip into underwriting losses.

book_subsections.title: Claims Handling as a Competitive Retention Engine
paragraphs: Many investors view claims departments purely as cost centers, yet at Chubb the claims organization is the ultimate customer-retention engine. When a commercial client suffers a factory fire or a Masterpiece homeowner faces a burst pipe in a historic residence, the speed, fairness, and technical competence of the claims adjuster determine whether that client renews for the next twenty years.

By keeping complex claims handling in-house rather than outsourcing to third-party administrators, Chubb controls both loss-adjustment expenses and customer satisfaction. That alignment is why Chubb consistently maintains industry-leading renewal retention even when competitors dangle 10% introductory price cuts.
